query: Which method can be used for high-temperature oxidation behaviour and phase stability, and why?

generation.hypothesis: In situ high‐temperature X‐ray diffraction (HTXRD) can be used to study high‐temperature oxidation behaviour and phase stability because it provides real-time monitoring of phase transformations and oxide formation during heating.
generation.material_initial_state: An as-synthesized high-entropy alloy in its primary single-phase state (e.g., BCC or B2, as determined at room temperature)
generation.intervention: Heating the material to high temperatures (such as 850–1100 °C) under controlled atmospheres (air or vacuum) while simultaneously collecting XRD data
generation.conditions: Controlled heating rates (e.g., ~15 °C/min) with periodic stabilization for acquisition of diffraction patterns, in either oxidizing (air) or inert (vacuum) environments
generation.structural_mediator: The formation of new oxide phases (e.g., MnO, Cr2O3, spinels) and phase transformation signals (shifts in lattice parameters or the appearance/disappearance of diffraction peaks) serve as mediators linking temperature to oxidation and phase stability
generation.mechanism: As temperature increases, atomic mobilities and diffusion rates increase, leading to oxidation and phase transitions. HTXRD detects these changes by recording variations in peak positions, intensities, and the emergence of new reflections, which directly correlate with the onset of oxide formation or the transformation into new phases.
generation.predicted_outcome: Distinct changes in the diffraction patterns (e.g., appearance of oxide peaks or shifts in peak positions) will be observed at specific high-temperature thresholds, indicating phase transformations and oxidation kinetics.
generation.baseline: The initial XRD pattern recorded at room temperature showing the primary phase with well-defined lattice parameters and no oxide-related peaks.
generation.boundary: Variations in heating rate or environmental conditions (e.g., air vs vacuum) may shift the temperature onset of oxidation or phase change, but the overall method should still capture the transformation sequence if it is effective.
generation.uncertainty: Exact temperatures at which changes occur may depend on the alloy composition and experimental setup; additionally, minor phases or low volume fraction oxides might be challenging to detect if below the instrument’s sensitivity.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare high-entropy alloy samples and perform a series of controlled heating experiments in an HTXRD setup under both air and vacuum conditions. Collect diffraction patterns at fixed temperature intervals throughout the heating cycle (e.g., every 50 °C) up to 1100 °C.
measurements: XRD patterns (peak positions, intensities, and widths) at each temperature interval
Detection and identification of emerging peaks corresponding to oxide phases or new structural phases
Monitoring of lattice parameter changes in the original phase
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If, across the entire temperature range and under both environments, no detectable changes in the diffraction patterns (e.g., no emergence of new peaks or systematic shifts in peak positions indicative of phase transformations or oxidation) are observed, then this would falsify the hypothesis that HTXRD is effective for monitoring high-temperature oxidation behaviour and phase stability.

Question: What are the time–temperature-dependent oxidation mechanisms and phase transformations of CrMnFeCoNi high-entropy alloy in vacuum and air environments, and how do they compare with thermodynamic predictions?. System: Equiatomic CrMnFeCoNi high-entropy alloy (20 at.% each of Cr, Co, Fe, Mn, Ni). Processing: Arc melting and drop casting of 3 N purity elements in a vacuum of ~7 × 10⁻⁴ Pa followed by argon refilling to ~8.4 × 10⁴ Pa; annealing at 900 °C for 48 h; cold rolling to 1.6 mm thickness; mechanical and mirror polishing with 1 μm diamond suspension for in situ analysis. Test conditions: In situ high-temperature X-ray diffraction (HTXRD) from 25 °C to 1100 °C at 15 °C/min heating rate with 5 min stabilization at 50 °C intervals; two environments: vacuum (~4.2 × 10⁻⁶ atm) and air (1.0 atm); CuKα radiation (λ = 0.154 nm), 40 kV, 40 mA, 2θ range 30–80°.
